# Validating the Measure {#sec-appendix-validate}

Experiment 1 plants structure in a *language* and measures a trained model's representation. However, one limitation with that approach is that it cannot tell a failure in the *measurement* from the learner model simply representing the language differently than the structure planted in the language. This appendix removes the ambiguity by planting $\mu$, $\alpha$, $\beta$, and $\gamma$ **directly in a representation**, with no model and no training, and passing the result to the same function the language models are measured with. Ground truth now sits at the level the measure operates on.

```{r}
#| label: setup-validate
#| include: false
val <- rd("validate_measure.csv")
v_rec <- val |> filter(n_obs == 24, d >= 768) |> group_by(planted_int) |>
  summarize(n = n(), measured = median(size_interaction),
            lo = quantile(size_interaction, .025), hi = quantile(size_interaction, .975),
            flagged = mean(size_interaction_excludes_zero), .groups = "drop")
v_null <- bind_rows(
  val |> filter(planted_int == 0) |> group_by(n_obs) |>
    summarize(effect = "interaction", med = median(size_interaction),
              p95 = quantile(size_interaction, .95),
              flagged = mean(size_interaction_excludes_zero), .groups = "drop"),
  val |> filter(planted_class == 0) |> group_by(n_obs) |>
    summarize(effect = "class effect", med = median(size_class),
              p95 = quantile(size_class, .95),
              flagged = mean(size_class_excludes_zero), .groups = "drop"),
  val |> filter(planted_item == 0) |> group_by(n_obs) |>
    summarize(effect = "item effect", med = median(size_item),
              p95 = quantile(size_item, .95),
              flagged = mean(size_item_excludes_zero), .groups = "drop"))
# False-positive rate of the re-split test BY WIDTH: how often a truly-zero effect's interval
# excludes zero. This is what says whether a small measured effect at a given width is a real
# detection or the test's own floor, and it tells the reader where the test is calibrated.
v_fp_d <- bind_rows(
  val |> filter(planted_int == 0, n_obs == 24) |> group_by(d) |>
    summarize(effect = "interaction", fp = mean(size_interaction_excludes_zero), .groups = "drop"),
  val |> filter(planted_class == 0, n_obs == 24) |> group_by(d) |>
    summarize(effect = "class", fp = mean(size_class_excludes_zero), .groups = "drop"),
  val |> filter(planted_item == 0, n_obs == 24) |> group_by(d) |>
    summarize(effect = "item", fp = mean(size_item_excludes_zero), .groups = "drop"))
fpget <- function(eff, dd) v_fp_d$fp[v_fp_d$effect == eff & v_fp_d$d == dd]
v_ov <- val |> filter(!is.na(leak_item_into_class), n_obs == 24, planted_overlap == 0) |>
  group_by(d) |> summarize(measured = median(leak_item_into_class),
                           lo = quantile(leak_item_into_class, .025),
                           hi = quantile(leak_item_into_class, .975),
                           chance = median(k_class / d), .groups = "drop")
# The power side: a KNOWN fraction of the class direction planted inside the item subspace. The
# measured overlap should rise above chance and be flagged outside its own random-orientation null.
v_ov_power <- val |> filter(!is.na(leak_item_into_class), n_obs == 24, planted_overlap > 0) |>
  group_by(d) |> summarize(measured = median(leak_item_into_class),
                           lo = quantile(leak_item_into_class, .025),
                           hi = quantile(leak_item_into_class, .975),
                           chance = median(k_class / d),
                           detected = mean(leak_item_into_class_outside %in% c(TRUE, "TRUE")),
                           .groups = "drop")
vget <- function(eff, obs, col) v_null[[col]][v_null$effect == eff & v_null$n_obs == obs]
```

The three components are drawn at random and then centered so each satisfies the constraints its role implies: $\alpha$ and $\beta$ sum to zero over their own index, $\gamma$ over both. Without that, a planted $\gamma$ would partly be an item or class main effect and the planted shares would be wrong before the measure saw them. Each is rescaled to hit a target share of the total squared length across the grid, under the same weighting the measure uses. Each mean is then observed $n$ times under isotropic noise, whose scale is set as a multiple of the mean squared length. The grid crosses the planted structure (the same factorial Experiment 1 runs, mapped into share space, plus the three compositions Experiment 2 measures), item counts from 27 to 180, two and four classes, widths from 8 to 2048, 10, 24, and 100 observations per item and class, three noise levels, planted-orthogonal and planted-non-orthogonal effects, and five seeds: `r cm(nrow(val))` runs.

At 24 observations per item and class, inside the 10-to-100 range in which the language-model item sets sit, the measured interaction matches the planted one across the whole range (Table \ref{tbl-val-recovery}), and is flagged in essentially every run where anything was planted and about one in twenty where nothing was.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-val-recovery
#| tbl-cap: "Recovery at 24 observations per item and class in 768 or more dimensions, pooled over noise levels, item counts, and widths. Brackets are the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles across runs."
v_rec |> filter(planted_int == 0 | planted_int > 0.02) |> head(12) |>
  transmute(`planted` = g(planted_int, 3),
            runs = n,
            `measured` = sprintf("%.4f [%.4f, %.4f]", measured, lo, hi),
            `flagged` = sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * flagged)) |>
  kbl(longtable = FALSE, booktabs = TRUE, align = "rrrr", linesep = "") |>
  kable_styling(font_size = 9)
```

All three effects read essentially zero when nothing is planted, at every sample size, and each is flagged at about the nominal 5% (Table \ref{tbl-val-null}): at 24 observations per item and class a true zero class effect reads `r g(vget("class effect", 24, "med"), 4)`. This calibration is what licenses reading the small metaphor class effect in @sec-exp2-results as real rather than as the floor: since a true zero reads essentially zero at this sample size, an interval that excludes zero separates even an effect as small as metaphor's from zero rather than measuring noise.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-val-null
#| tbl-cap: "What the measure reports when an effect is planted at exactly zero, by observations per item and class, pooled over every other axis of the validation grid."
v_null |>
  transmute(effect, observations = n_obs,
            median = g(med, 5), `95th pct` = g(p95, 4),
            flagged = ifelse(is.na(flagged), "---", sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * flagged))) |>
  arrange(effect, observations) |>
  kbl(longtable = FALSE, booktabs = TRUE, align = "lrrrr", linesep = "") |>
  kable_styling(font_size = 9)
```

The rate at which a genuine zero is nonetheless flagged varies with width and effect rather than holding at the nominal 5% (Table \ref{tbl-val-fpd}). The class effect is the most liberal, and most so at the smallest width, where a true zero is flagged `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * fpget("class", 8))` of the time; the item effect is the most conservative, falling to `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * fpget("item", 2048))` at the widest. No setting exceeds ten percent, and pooled across widths the class and interaction are a little more liberal than the item effect. This is the floor the Experiment 1 results at small width are read against, so a lone flag at $d = 8$ is weak on its own. The language-model results sit at $d \geq 768$, where the rate is mildly liberal at worst, and each rests on the effect clearing zero in all six models, which even an eight-percent per-model rate would not produce by chance.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-val-fpd
#| tbl-cap: "How often a component planted at exactly zero is flagged, by width and by effect."
v_fp_d |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = effect, values_from = fp) |>
  transmute(`width d` = d,
            item = sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * item),
            class = sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * class),
            interaction = sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * interaction)) |>
  kbl(longtable = FALSE, booktabs = TRUE, align = "rrrr", linesep = "") |>
  kable_styling(font_size = 9)
```

With the item and class effects planted orthogonal, the measured overlap tracks $r/d$ closely and sits a little below it (Table \ref{tbl-val-overlap}). This is the number that Experiment 2's overlaps are read against: at $d = 2048$ a genuinely orthogonal pair reads `r g(v_ov$measured[v_ov$d == 2048], 5)`, and the values reported in @sec-exp2-results are `r sprintf("%.1f to %.1f times", min(llm_deep$leak, na.rm = TRUE) / v_ov$measured[v_ov$d == 2048], max(llm_deep$leak, na.rm = TRUE) / v_ov$measured[v_ov$d == 2048])` that.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-val-overlap
#| tbl-cap: "Measured item-class overlap when the two effects are planted orthogonal, at 24 observations per item and class. *Measured* is the median over the runs at that width with the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles in brackets. The *chance* column is the analytic level of Appendix \\ref{sec-appendix-math}."
v_ov |>
  transmute(`width d` = d, measured = ci(measured, lo, hi, 5),
            `analytic chance` = g(chance, 5)) |>
  kbl(longtable = FALSE, booktabs = TRUE, align = "rrr", linesep = "") |>
  kable_styling(font_size = 9)
```

The orthogonal case shows the overlap does not cry wolf; the planted-non-orthogonal case shows it does not miss. With a known fraction of the class direction placed inside the item subspace, the measured overlap rises well above the chance level and falls outside its own null in the large majority of runs (Table \ref{tbl-val-power}): at $d = 2048$ a planted-non-orthogonal pair reads `r g(v_ov_power$measured[v_ov_power$d == 2048], 4)` against a chance of `r g(v_ov_power$chance[v_ov_power$d == 2048], 5)`, detected in `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * v_ov_power$detected[v_ov_power$d == 2048])` of runs. So a reported overlap is one the measure can place at chance when the effects are orthogonal and lift above it when the non-orthogonality is real, which is what makes the Experiment 2 overlaps interpretable in both directions.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-val-power
#| tbl-cap: "Measured item-class overlap when a fraction of the class direction is planted INSIDE the item subspace (non-orthogonal), at 24 observations per item and class. *Measured* is the median over the runs at that width with the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles in brackets; *chance* is the analytic random-orientation level; *detected* is the fraction of runs whose overlap falls outside that null's 95% interval."
v_ov_power |>
  transmute(`width d` = d, measured = ci(measured, lo, hi, 4), chance = g(chance, 5),
            detected = sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * detected)) |>
  kbl(longtable = FALSE, booktabs = TRUE, align = "rrrr", linesep = "") |>
  kable_styling(font_size = 9)
```

{{< pagebreak >}}

# Crowding and Orthogonality {#sec-appendix-capacity}

Whether the item and class effects come out orthogonal depends on whether the representation had room for them to be, which is a fact about crowding rather than about the language. The languages are held fixed across these runs; only the hidden width changes. @fig-capacity shows the overlap against crowding and @tbl-toy the interaction size and both overlaps at each crowding value.

```{r}
#| label: fig-capacity
#| fig-width: 3.2
#| fig-height: 2.5
#| out-width: "70%"
#| fig-cap: "Item-class overlap against crowding, by activation, over the 7,560 artificial-language runs. Crowding is the rank the structure needs divided by the hidden width. The dashed line is the median upper end of the null for an arbitrarily oriented effect. Both axes are logarithmic."
ACT2 <- c(linear = UO[["green2"]], ReLU = UO[["gold"]])
# one chance line, not one per condition: the two differ slightly because the class subspace
# rank is estimated, and drawing both makes a zigzag that reads as structure when it is not
floor_line <- toy_cap |> group_by(capacity) |> summarize(floor = median(floor), .groups = "drop")
ggplot(toy_cap, aes(capacity, overlap, color = act)) +
  geom_line(data = floor_line, mapping = aes(capacity, floor), inherit.aes = FALSE,
            color = UO[["grey"]], linetype = 2, linewidth = .5) +
  geom_line(linewidth = .6) + geom_point(size = 1.5) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.135, y = 0.032, label = "chance", size = 2.5,
           color = UO[["grey"]], hjust = 0) +
  scale_color_manual(values = ACT2, name = NULL) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(.125, .25, .5, 1, 2)) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = scales::label_number(drop0trailing = TRUE)) +
  labs(x = "crowding (structure rank / hidden width)", y = "item-class overlap (log)") +
  theme_paper(8)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-toy
#| tbl-cap: "Interaction size and the two overlaps by activation and crowding, over the 7,560 artificial-language runs. Crowding is the rank the structure needs divided by the hidden width; each crowding value corresponds to one width, from 128 down to 8. *Interaction* is the median share of the representation over the runs in the row, their interquartile range in brackets, and how many have a re-split 95% interval excluding zero. The overlap columns give the median fraction surviving the projection, then in parentheses how many times its own null median that is and how many runs fall outside that null. The linear arm's interaction stays below the 2% floor at which orientations are reported, so its last column is empty."
toy_cap |>
  transmute(condition = act, crowding = g(capacity, 3), runs = n,
            interaction = sz_int,
            `item-class overlap` = ov_item,
            # the linear arm's interaction stays under the 2% floor at which orientations are
            # reported, so there is no fitted direction to place
            `interaction overlap` = ifelse(act == "linear", "---", ov_int)) |>
  arrange(condition, crowding) |>
  kbl(booktabs = TRUE, align = "lrrrrr", linesep = "", escape = FALSE) |>
  kable_styling(latex_options = c("HOLD_position"), font_size = 7)
```

Two further properties of the language move the composition, and are given here rather than folded into @fig-toy (Table \ref{tbl-lang}). Context competes with the interaction for room: the more of the language that is context, the smaller the interaction's share of the item-by-class structure. And the balance the language strikes between the item and the class is reflected in the representation, the measured item share rising with the planted one.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-lang
#| tbl-cap: "How two other properties of the artificial language move the composition of the item-by-class structure, under ReLU, pooled over widths. Rows within a property partition the same runs. Values are medians of the three shares over the runs in the row."
toy_bylang |>
  transmute(property, level, runs,
            item = g(item, 3), class = g(class, 3), interaction = g(interaction, 3)) |>
  kbl(booktabs = TRUE, align = "llrrrr", linesep = "") |>
  kable_styling(latex_options = c("HOLD_position"), font_size = 8) |>
  collapse_rows(1, latex_hline = "major", valign = "top")
```

Training-token counts are approximate; the OPT-BabyLM models train for 20 epochs over a 100M-word corpus, so their effective token exposure is roughly twenty times the corpus size. *Layers* counts the transformer blocks, and the measure is applied to each block's output plus the embedding layer."
```{r}
tibble::tribble(
  ~family,  ~model,          ~params, ~width, ~layers, ~`training data`,     ~`tokens`,
  "BabyLM", "opt-babylm-125m", "125M",   768,      12, "BabyLM (child-available)", "~2B",
  "BabyLM", "opt-babylm-350m", "350M",  1024,      24, "BabyLM (child-available)", "~2B",
  "BabyLM", "opt-babylm-1.3B", "1.3B",  2048,      24, "BabyLM (child-available)", "~2B",
  "Pythia", "pythia-160m",     "160M",   768,      12, "the Pile",                 "~300B",
  "Pythia", "pythia-410m",     "410M",  1024,      24, "the Pile",                 "~300B",
  "Pythia", "pythia-1.4b",     "1.4B",  2048,      24, "the Pile",                 "~300B") |>
  kbl(longtable = FALSE, booktabs = TRUE, align = "llrrrlr", linesep = "") |>
  kable_styling(font_size = 9) |>
  collapse_rows(columns = 1, latex_hline = "major")
```

The six models are listed in @tbl-models. The two families are matched on width rather than on parameter count, which is what the measure is sensitive to: the chance level for overlap is the class subspace rank over the width (Appendix \ref{sec-appendix-math}), so a comparison across models of different width has to be read against different chance levels. Pairing at 768, 1024, and 2048 removes that from the family comparison.

They differ in two ways that matter elsewhere in the paper. The training corpora differ by more than two orders of magnitude in size, which is the manipulation of interest. And they position tokens differently: Pythia uses rotary embeddings, applied inside attention, while OPT learns absolute position embeddings added at the input. Appendix \ref{sec-appendix-positions} uses that difference to rule out absolute position as the source of the interaction.

{{< pagebreak >}}

# The Decomposition {#sec-appendix-math}

## The item-by-class means {#sec-appendix-math-grid}

![Each word in each class is observed in many contexts, and those observations are averaged within the pairing to give one of the item-by-class means. Every one of them is a vector in $\mathbb{R}^d$, and every item appears in every class.](fig-grid.pdf){#fig-grid width="100%"}

A word used in a given class is observed in many contexts, and the representation differs a little in each. Averaging those observations within the pairing gives one of the item-by-class means: for items $i \in \{1,\dots,I\}$ crossed with classes $c \in \{1,\dots,C\}$, $M[i,c] \in \mathbb{R}^d$ is the mean representation of item $i$ in class $c$ (@fig-grid). An item observed in only one class is dropped, as is an item with fewer than 10 tokens in either class, so the set is complete and every mean rests on a comparable number of observations. Because every item appears at every class, the means arrange into $I$ by $C$ positions, and the rest of this appendix calls that arrangement the grid when what matters is the positions rather than the vectors sitting at them. The variation across contexts that the averaging sets aside is not discarded; it is what the two splits of @sec-measure are drawn from.

## The decomposition as a projection {#sec-appendix-math-proj}

![Centering, drawn for a single hidden dimension read across the whole grid. The all-ones direction is where every position takes the same value, so it carries no differences and no variance, and $\mu$ is the projection onto it. Removing it leaves a hyperplane of dimension $N-1$, and every remaining component is a displacement inside it. The dashed copy is that displacement moved to the origin, where it lies in the hyperplane.](fig-projection.pdf){#fig-projection width="82%"}

Two spaces are in play. The representations themselves live in $\mathbb{R}^d$. The decomposition happens in the grid index space: fix one hidden dimension, read it across all $IC$ positions of the grid, and it is a vector in $\mathbb{R}^{IC}$ (@fig-projection). Everything below is that operation carried out once per hidden dimension, with the results stacked back up into the vectors $\alpha_i$, $\beta_c$, and $\gamma_{ic}$.

In that space the all-ones direction is the one in which every position of the grid takes the same value. Moving along it adds the same amount everywhere and creates no difference between any two positions, so it is the direction along which nothing distinguishes anything, and $\mu$ is the projection onto it. Removing it leaves the orthogonal complement, and the three remaining components are displacements inside that complement rather than raw values.

Each component is fixed by two choices, one per axis: along the item axis either average or center, and along the class axis the same. Averaging keeps what is common and discards what makes positions differ along that axis; centering does the reverse. The four combinations are the four components of @eq-decomp:

|               | varies over items | varies over classes |
|:--------------|:-----------------:|:-------------------:|
| $\mu$         |        no         |         no          |
| $\alpha_i$    |        yes        |         no          |
| $\beta_c$     |        no         |         yes         |
| $\gamma_{ic}$ |        yes        |         yes         |

So $\alpha_i$ is what holds of an item in both classes, $\beta_c$ is what holds of a class for every item, and $\gamma_{ic}$ is what varies along both at once, which is why it cannot be a fact about either one alone. Since averaging and centering along an axis add back to what was there, the four reconstruct $M[i,c]$ exactly, and they are mutually orthogonal.

Centering an axis costs one dimension, the all-ones direction along it. The four components therefore occupy $1$, $I{-}1$, $C{-}1$, and $(I{-}1)(C{-}1)$ of the grid's $IC$ positions, which is why two classes leave $\beta$ a single direction whatever $I$ is. Nothing is left over as error: $\gamma$ is not a residual in the sense of a model that failed to fit, but the part of the representation belonging to the pairing of a particular item with a particular class.

Two consequences are used in the body. First, $\sum_i\alpha_i = 0$, $\sum_c\beta_c = 0$, and $\sum_i\gamma_{ic} = \sum_c\gamma_{ic} = 0$ follow from the centering rather than being imposed as constraints. Second, an **additive** set of means, one of the form $M[i,c] = A(i) + B(c)$, has $\gamma = 0$ *identically*: writing $\bar A$ and $\bar B$ for the averages, $\mu = \bar A + \bar B$, $\alpha_i = A(i) - \bar A$, $\beta_c = B(c) - \bar B$, and the remainder cancels exactly. This is the algebra behind the linear condition of Experiment 1: its population means, the pairing means taken over the same context distribution everywhere, are additive and its interaction is zero. What it is measured on is the means of its observed sample, which can also hold a trace of each pairing's own contexts (Experiment 1, Results), so the floor the linear arm provides is read off the planted-zero languages, not deduced.

## Sizes {#sec-appendix-math-sizes}

![How many positions of the grid each component occupies. $\alpha_i$ does not depend on the class, so it occupies all $C$ positions of its row; $\beta_c$ does not depend on the item, so it occupies all $I$ positions of its column; $\gamma_{ic}$ takes its own value at every position and is never repeated.](fig-replication.pdf){#fig-replication width="100%"}

Because the three components are mutually orthogonal, their squared lengths add rather than overlapping, and the total squared length across the grid partitions exactly:

$$
\sum_{i,c}\lVert M[i,c]-\mu\rVert^{2}
= C\sum_{i}\lVert\alpha_i\rVert^{2}
+ I\sum_{c}\lVert\beta_c\rVert^{2}
+ \sum_{i,c}\lVert\gamma_{ic}\rVert^{2},
$$

$C$ and $I$ are not a choice of scaling. They are how many positions of the grid each component occupies (@fig-replication): $\alpha_i$ does not depend on the class, so it sits at all $C$ positions of its row, and $\beta_c$ does not depend on the item, so it sits at all $I$ positions of its column. Every one of the $I$ items is displaced by the same $\beta_c$, so the displacement present in the grid is $I$ copies of it. The interaction is simply summed because it takes its own value at every position and is never repeated. Dividing all three by $IC$ would report averages per position instead of totals and leave every share unchanged; what the occupancy counts rule out is weighting the three differently from one another.

Sizes are reported as shares of the total. All three terms scale linearly in $I$, so the shares do not depend on how many items there are and are comparable across categories of different size.

The partition above is of the item-by-class structure, which has already averaged the contexts away, so it leaves open how much of the representation that structure is. Splitting each observation into its pairing mean and its deviation from it, and using the fact that deviations from a mean sum to zero, gives a second exact partition one level up:

$$
\sum_{x}\lVert x - \bar x\rVert^{2}
= \underbrace{\sum_{i,c}\sum_{x \in (i,c)} \lVert x - \hat M[i,c]\rVert^{2}}_{\text{within a pairing}}
+ \underbrace{\sum_{i,c} n_{ic}\lVert \hat M[i,c] - \bar x\rVert^{2}}_{\text{between pairings}} .
$$

The raw between fraction overstates the item-by-class structure, because $\hat M[i,c]$ is itself an average of $n_{ic}$ observations and carries $d\sigma^2/n_{ic}$ of context noise that lands in the between term. The bias falls as tokens per item rise, so it differs across categories and would not be comparable between them. We therefore report the variance-component form: the within mean square estimates the context variance, the between mean square estimates that plus $n_0$ times the true spread of the pairing means with $n_0$ the effective group size of the unbalanced design, and the difference gives the spread alone. Planting no structure at all, the raw fraction reads $0.081$ at 12 observations per pairing and $0.005$ at 200, while the corrected one reads zero at both.

Because the corrected quantities are variance components rather than weighted sums, they compose with the sizes: each size times that structure's share gives that component's share of the representation, and the three plus the context term account for it entirely.

## The overlaps and their chance level {#sec-appendix-math-overlap}

The sizes say how much of the representation each component accounts for and nothing about direction. Two components can both be large whether or not they occupy the same directions, and separability is the second question: a word's representation is an item part plus a class part only if the two can be varied independently, which requires them to lie on distinct axes. That question lives in $\mathbb{R}^d$, not in the grid index space the sizes were computed in, and unlike the sizes it does not partition, because each overlap is a relation between two particular components rather than a share of one whole.

Each overlap projects one component into the subspace another occupies:

| projected | into the subspace of         |
|:----------|:-----------------------------|
| $\alpha$  | $\beta$                      |
| $\beta$   | $\alpha$                     |
| $\gamma$  | $\alpha$ and $\beta$ jointly |

The first two are not redundant with each other. One direction and thirty-odd are very different targets to land in by chance, and the chance level below is what puts them on a comparable footing.

Subspaces are orthonormal bases from the leading right singular vectors, with rank set by the participation ratio $r = \operatorname{round}\!\big((\sum_k\lambda_k)^2/\sum_k\lambda_k^2\big)$ of the scatter eigenvalues, capped at the algebraic maxima above. The participation ratio counts directions discounted by how much each carries: it returns 1 when all the spread lies along one direction and $k$ when it is even across $k$ of them. With two classes $\beta$ spans one direction, so $r_{\text{class}} = 1$ throughout Experiment 2.

Writing $S$ for the $d \times r$ basis and $V$ for the component being projected, the overlap is $\lVert V S\rVert_F^2 / \lVert V\rVert_F^2$. $V$ is complete, every vector of the component at full dimension; only $S$ is rank-truncated. So the rank enters through the target alone, which is why it fixes the chance level without altering any measured overlap.

The overlap is a squared cosine. For one vector and one direction, $\langle v, u\rangle^2/\lVert v\rVert^2 = \cos^2\theta$ exactly, so the ratio is a length-weighted mean of $\cos^2\theta_i$ over the vectors of $V$, with $\theta_i$ the angle between vector $i$ and the nearest direction in $S$. Weighting by squared length keeps items with small, poorly determined effects from moving the number. The square root inverts to an angle, which is the more legible scale near the floor: an overlap of $0.19$ is $64^\circ$ and one of $0.0056$ is $86^\circ$, nearly perpendicular rather than merely small.

Squaring rather than summing the signed dot products is not cosmetic. Because $\sum_i \alpha_i = 0$, the signed version is $\langle \sum_i \alpha_i, \beta\rangle = 0$ identically, whatever the geometry: items leaning one way along the class axis cancel those leaning the other. Squaring is also what makes the two directions of a component count equally, which is what the question requires, since projecting the class direction out costs an item the same either way.

The chance level is not zero. For a randomly oriented $V$,

$$
\mathbb{E}\big[\lVert V S\rVert_F^2\big] = \operatorname{tr}(V^{\top}V)/d \cdot r
\;\Longrightarrow\;
\mathbb{E}[\text{overlap}] = r/d ,
$$

whatever $V$'s rank or shape. At $d = 2048$ that is $0.0005$ for a one-direction class subspace, and Appendix \ref{sec-appendix-validate} recovers it empirically, a planted-orthogonal pair landing a little below its own $r/d$ at every width. Any overlap has to be read against that number, which moves by two orders of magnitude across the widths used in this paper.

The measure is exactly invariant to per-dimension rescaling, which the standardization absorbs, and to orthogonal rotation of already-standardized data. It is **not** invariant to general linear reparameterization: we do not whiten, because whitening would make a linear representation read separable in any basis and would discard the basis the model actually computes in. Overlap values are therefore basis-relative, while the sizes and their growth with depth do not depend on the choice.

{{< pagebreak >}}

# Deepest-Layer Measurements {#sec-appendix-llm}

Table \ref{tbl-llm} gives the deepest-layer values behind the curves of @fig-llm, together with the null each overlap is read against.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-llm
#| tbl-cap: "Deepest-layer measurements, one row per model. The two overlaps are the fraction of the item effect lying in the class subspace and the fraction of the interaction lying in the span of the two main effects, each followed in parentheses by how many times its own rotation null's median it is. That null holds the effect fixed and rotates the target subspace at random 200 times. The class effect and the interaction are shares of the item-by-class structure, with each model's re-split 95% interval in brackets."
llm |> group_by(construction, model) |>
  filter(layer == max(layer)) |> ungroup() |>
  arrange(construction, family, scale) |>
  # One row per model. A median across the six hid exactly what the six are being compared for,
  # and the sizes' re-split intervals are far narrower than the spread across models, so pooling
  # them reported a precision that belonged to a single measurement rather than to the set.
  # Each overlap is against its own model's null rather than r/d: the two differ, since r/d
  # assumes the subspace has its algebraic maximum rank while the projection uses the rank
  # actually fitted, roughly half of it for the marginal subspace.
  transmute(class = shortname(construction),
            model = paste(family, size),
            `item-class overlap` = ov1(leak, leak_null_med, 4),
            `interaction overlap` = ov1(leak_int, leak_int_null_med, 3),
            `class effect` = ci(size_class, size_class_lo, size_class_hi),
            `interaction` = ci(size_int, size_int_lo, size_int_hi)) |>
  kbl(longtable = FALSE, booktabs = TRUE, align = "llrrrr", linesep = "") |>
  kable_styling(font_size = 7) |>
  collapse_rows(1, latex_hline = "major", valign = "top")
```

{{< pagebreak >}}

# Positional Embeddings Are Not the Source {#sec-appendix-positions}

One architectural explanation of the interaction has to be ruled out before it can be read as a fact about lexical representation. OPT-BabyLM adds a *learned absolute position embedding* at the input. The two classes of a linguistic category are not positionally interchangeable in a sentence, since subjects precede objects and nouns and verbs occupy different slots, so a representation that varies with position varies with the class. If that is what the decomposition is picking up, the interaction would be an artifact of where words sit rather than of how they are represented.

We re-extracted every OPT-BabyLM model with *decoder.embed_positions* zeroed and measured it identically. The ablation was verified per model rather than assumed: with the embedding zeroed, the same token at two different offsets must give identical layer-0 states, and it does, in every model (drift $0.0$ to machine precision). Pythia has no such module, so there is nothing to zero there.

The right quantity is the class effect's share of class-relevant structure, the class effect divided by the sum of the class effect and the interaction, which we call the *portable fraction*. If positions were manufacturing the interaction, removing them should leave a larger share of what distinguishes the two classes in a direction shared across words. Absolute sizes cannot be compared here: zeroing the embeddings in a model that was trained with them is a heavy intervention, and it shrinks every component at once, the class effect included.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-posabl
#| tbl-cap: "Trained OPT-BabyLM at the deepest layer, with absolute position embeddings intact and zeroed. Sizes are shares of the item-by-class structure and the portable fraction is the class effect divided by the sum of the class effect and the interaction."
rd("llm_unified_form_ablation.csv") |>
  filter(grepl("babylm", model), grepl("^pretrained", init)) |>
  group_by(model, init) |>
  slice_max(layer, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  ungroup() |>
  transmute(model = sub(".*/", "", sub("-20eps-seed964", "", model)),
            positions = ifelse(grepl("noposemb$", init), "zeroed", "intact"),
            class = std_size_class, interaction = std_size_interaction,
            portable = std_size_class / (std_size_class + std_size_interaction)) |>
  arrange(match(model, c("opt-babylm-125m", "opt-babylm-350m", "opt-babylm-1.3B")),
          desc(positions)) |>
  transmute(model, positions, `class` = g(class, 3), `interaction` = g(interaction, 3),
            `portable fraction` = g(portable, 3)) |>
  kbl(longtable = FALSE, booktabs = TRUE, align = "llrrr", linesep = "") |>
  kable_styling(font_size = 9)
```

Removing the position embeddings makes these representations *less* separable, not more. The portable fraction falls in every model, from 0.439 to 0.264, from 0.468 to 0.253, and from 0.333 to 0.198 (Table \ref{tbl-posabl}). Whatever the absolute position embedding contributes, it is contributing to the part of class structure that *is* carried by a shared direction. Take it away and what remains is more word-specific, not less. The interaction is not an artifact of position.

A second line of evidence points the same way and needs no ablation at all. Pythia never had an absolute position embedding to remove, and its portable fractions are 0.253, 0.287 and 0.262, at or below every intact OPT-BabyLM value. The family without the mechanism shows the phenomenon at least as strongly as the family with it. An explanation resting on absolute position embeddings would have to account for the models that do not have them.

We tested this for part of speech, the category where the positional worry is sharpest because noun and verb uses of a form occupy systematically different sentence positions. Grammatical role carries the same concern for the same reason, and behaves the same way. Metaphor does not, since literal and figurative uses of a word are not positionally distinguished.
